name: Bioorganic Chemistry
tagline: Natural products, biosynthesis, and organic chemistry of biological systems.
seo_title: Bioorganic Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Bioorganic Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in natural products, biosynthesis, enzyme mechanisms and bioorthogonal chemistry.

definition.lead: Bioorganic chemistry uses the tools of organic chemistry to understand how living systems make and use molecules.
definition.body: It studies how enzymes catalyse reactions, how cells build natural products and how small molecules can probe or switch biological processes. It connects the flask to the cell.

facts.label: Emil Fischer proposes the lock-and-key model of enzymes
the Miller–Urey experiment makes amino acids from simple gases

branches.name: Natural products
branches.summary: Molecules made by plants, fungi, bacteria and marine life.

branches.name: Biosynthesis
branches.example: Polyketide synthases working like assembly lines.

branches.name: Enzyme mechanisms
branches.summary: The organic chemistry inside an active site.
branches.example: The catalytic triad of serine proteases.

branches.name: Bioorthogonal chemistry
branches.summary: Reactions that run inside living systems without disturbing them.
branches.example: Labelling sugars on the surface of cancer cells.

branches.name: Peptides
branches.summary: Short chains of amino acids as drugs and tools.

branches.name: Carbohydrates
branches.summary: The chemistry of sugars and glycans.
branches.example: Sugar coats that cells use to recognize each other.

branches.name: Nucleic acid chemistry
branches.summary: Modified building blocks for DNA and RNA.

timeline.title: Lock and key
timeline.text: Emil Fischer proposes that an enzyme fits its substrate like a key in a lock.
timeline.why: The first model of molecular recognition.

timeline.title: Sugars and purines
timeline.text: Emil Fischer receives the Nobel Prize for his work on sugars and purines.
timeline.why: Organic chemistry applied to the molecules of life.

timeline.title: The Miller–Urey experiment
timeline.text: Stanley Miller and Harold Urey make amino acids by sparking a mixture of simple gases.
timeline.why: Showed that building blocks of life can form spontaneously.

timeline.title: Induced fit
timeline.text: Daniel Koshland proposes that enzymes change shape when they bind.

timeline.title: An enzyme made in the lab
timeline.text: Bernd Gutte and Bruce Merrifield synthesize the enzyme ribonuclease A.
timeline.why: A working enzyme built entirely by chemists.

timeline.title: Catalytic RNA
timeline.text: Thomas Cech discovers that RNA can act as a catalyst.
timeline.why: Not all biological catalysts are proteins.

timeline.title: Bioorthogonal chemistry
timeline.text: Carolyn Bertozzi coins the term for reactions that work inside living systems.

timeline.title: Modified RNA
timeline.text: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman show modified nucleosides reduce immune reactions to mRNA.
timeline.why: A key step toward mRNA vaccines.

timeline.title: Click and bioorthogonal chemistry
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Bertozzi, Meldal and Sharpless.
timeline.why: Reliable reactions from the flask to the living cell.
